title: How To Avoid Holiday Misbehavior
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin offers three strategies to prevent the predictable rise in misbehavior as holiday break approaches, arguing that the phenomenon is common but not inevitable if teachers act before it starts. First, review the classroom management plan more frequently than usual (at least twice a week), stating the promise of consistent follow-through so students see nothing changes despite the approaching vacation. Second, deliberately slow down physical pace, speech, and transitions, because a teacher's energy sets the room's energy and calm modeling counteracts rising excitement. Third, keep academic expectations and workload high through the last day rather than easing off, scheduling major projects and tests near the end so students stay engaged rather than sensing that 'vacation starts before vacation.' He frames maintaining this rigor through the holidays not as being a 'scrooge' but as what separates good teachers from the rest.
points: Review your classroom management plan at least twice a week in the weeks before a break, erring toward more detail rather than less.
Deliberately slow your pace, speech, and movements before break — your energy sets your students' energy, especially as excitement rises.
Keep major tests, essays, and projects scheduled near the last day of school rather than easing off, since students sense when 'vacation starts before vacation.'
Wintry or seasonal activities are fine, but the standard for quality work and effort should never drop, even during the final days before break.
Maintaining rigor through the holidays isn't being a 'scrooge' — it's what separates good teachers from the rest and lets you enjoy your own break with a peaceful classroom.
quotes: Misbehavior tends to increase as we edge closer to holiday break. It’s a phenomenon as old as Santa and just as predictable. But it isn’t inevitable.
You’ll also want to review your plan often. Two days per week minimum, if not every day. After a more detailed, initial reteaching of your plan, subsequent reviews should only take a few minutes.
Moving fast, talking fast, and rushing through lessons and routines always causes worsening behavior. The difference in slowing your mind and body can be profound.
Students take their cue from you. Your energy determines the energy in the room. The more hyperactive and tense they are, the more relaxed and unhurried you should become.
But this signals to students that vacation starts before vacation—if you get my snow drift. Much better to have projects due and important tests and essays scheduled on the last day or so.
Students are getting pummeled on every side with messages that school is almost out and freedom and fun are soon to begin. You must be different than the normal teaching crowd.
